extracted.intended_audience: artists, art students, critics, and informed readers of painting and art theory
extracted.subtask_short: critique of landscape and architectural painting
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for painting—especially landscape and architectural subjects—focusing on fidelity to nature, national/locale feeling, drawing, colour, composition, and truthful treatment of architectural detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conveyance of the spirit of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract of decoration should have 'the spirit of the reality' rather than merely imitating surface details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is given where the artist catches the spirit of Gothic or Flemish architecture rather than laboriously copying ornament. The ideal is conveying the impression and soul of the subject, not mechanical reproduction of detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic depiction of architectural context
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists must draw whole cities and buildings, not only isolated mouldings, walls, windows, or decorative parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid producing technically correct mouldings or buttresses while failing to give the sense of a cathedral or the city as an organized whole; prefer compositions that show the unity and scale of architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of antiquarian feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Antiquarian feeling ought to be 'pure, earnest, and natural' rather than affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine historical sensibility and a vigorous imagination are virtues; decoration or antiquarian subject-matter should arise from honest feeling, not from fashionable or shallow affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study from nature (drapery, form, and detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drapery, folds, and forms should be studied out from nature rather than invented or conventionalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: no single fold of drapery studied from nature; sketchy, underdeveloped forms indicate wasting of power. Proper anatomical and material study is necessary to sustain original talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful handling of light and shade
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'violent conventionalism of light and shade' and the use of identical, arbitrary tones across different materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shadows and modelling must reflect the true behaviour of light on flesh, dress, and stone; using the same 'stucco color' everywhere is a sign of weakness. Varied, observed tonal relationships are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint in ornament and correctness of proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attain dignity by 'inordinate bulk of decorated parts'; dignity is reached by purity of proportion and majesty of line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerated, grotesque, or fantastical ornament (colossal cusps, monstrous machicolations) is a sign of childish fantasticism; proportion and line should govern decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for architectural truth and responsible invention
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'treason' to invent architectural features unless the invention is better than existing examples or genuinely differs in kind; if composing, designs should be such as 'the architect would applaud.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When architecture is the subject, artists should prioritize faithful record and understanding of structures. Invent only with purpose; do not replace real, vanishing monuments with ill-digested fancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and treatment that preserve actuality's nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist's selection of place, treatment, and incident should produce a noble picture 'without deviation from one line of the actual truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The highest imaginative achievement is to make a powerful picture while remaining true to the observed reality; this includes chosen composition, incident, and pictorial treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and 'laconic truth' in drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'right wit of drawing' is concise truth—not hyperbole, not violence, not frivolity, but well-expressed simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing should be expressive yet restrained; overstatement weakens, whereas laconic, accurate lines convey both measure and soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity of intention and honesty of system
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist's work should show honest purpose: the main lines of the real design must be present, with solidity and careful observation of hollows and undercuttings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive example: Roberts's main lines and sense of solidity are commended; technical dexterity should be allied to truthful observation and a coherent system of execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper value relationships and avoidance of jarring contrasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid careless juxtaposition of very light objects immediately in front of very dark areas (e.g., 'a white column coming out of a blue mist').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such artifices reveal poverty of conception and deficient habit of study; value organization must be considered to preserve impressiveness and colour harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough, varied study (including rapid and finished studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketches alone are not enough; the artist needs both accurate records and 'downright studies' including rapid blotted works that capture singular impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: producing only uniformly finished sketches that lack study of genuine hues and the unity of majestic impressions. Both patient record and quick impression studies are valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest and accurate colour (avoid cold, waxy, or opaque handling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colouring should be true; avoid cold, waxy, opaque tones and the unjustifiable use of violent black in deep shades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier warm, transparent priming (e.g., bituminous browns under whites) is preferable to later cold finish. Colour must reflect observed light and material, not studio conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of figures with ambient light and colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures must be blended with surrounding hues and lighting conditions, not inserted as violent, isolated spots of local colour painted from models in dead light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: foreground figures added merely as bright local colour (caftans, pipes) that contradict the light of the scene. Figures should be painted with reference to the scene's lighting and palette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting 'from and of nature' to achieve verity
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist should aim to 'paint not a fine picture but an impressive and known verity'—genuineness of hue and effect derived from nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honest, determined painting from nature supplies the genuineness of effect that elevates pictures beyond mere technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of affectation; preference for common-sense composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Good composition bears a 'look of common-sense and rationality' and avoids mannered affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stanfield praised for rational, unsentimental approaches; affectation or unnecessary drama undermines credibility—even when dramatic subject-matter is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive, weather-true skies
rubrics_metrics.description: Skies must be decisive and expressive (joyfulness of rest or majesty of storm); indecisive skies that don't commit to a weather state are defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sky should reinforce the scene's mood; hesitating or morbid-purple skies (or ambiguous weather) reduce the picture's appeal and narrative clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material truth: weathering, dirt, and the value of impurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists must recognize the expressive value of dirt and weathering (old boats, lichen, soiled clothes). Clean, new-looking objects often signal inauthenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict the true textures and impurities of life—weather-beaten boats, lichened rocks, soiled clothing—to enhance realism and emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationality and native experience as a source of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Great painters render what they 'had seen and felt from early childhood'—expression, types of countenance, costume, colour, and accessories tend to be those of the painter's native land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists achieve depth by working from long familiarity; attempting to paint convincingly entirely outside one's native perceptual ground often leads to failure or loss of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape choice: prefer subjects allied to the artist's feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: While landscape is less bound by nationality, painters should prefer fields that recall the feelings of their native landscapes; do not attempt to impose an alien spirit on place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle spares artists and critics from false compositions (e.g., inappropriate classical insertions); the most affecting landscapes retain the painter's authentic feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation in drawing and light before colour experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Secure drawing, quantity of form, and expression of atmosphere should be attained before introducing complicated or brilliant colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's Yorkshire drawings are commended as examples where avoiding colour difficulty allowed decisive drawing and atmospheric expression—use drawing as a foundation for later colour experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and emotional coherence in large compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Large works must avoid being overwhelmed with quantity of material at the expense of emotion; elements (foliage, architecture, water) must be integrated so the viewer knows where to look and what to feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: hybrid pictures that sacrifice foliage to architecture or vice versa, producing confusion (e.g., works that are 'neither sea, nor river, nor lake' and that lose emotional focus). Large compositions require careful unity of purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seize the actual character of foreign lands when painting them
rubrics_metrics.description: When painting abroad, artists should aim to seize the actual, local character of the country rather than only borrowing grand conceptions or general ideas of size and form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: France rewarded Turner with material congenial to his taste; Switzerland often supplied general notions rather than particular character. Successful foreign work depends on honest acquisition of local particulars.
